1. Introduction & Epidemiology

Tintinalli Ch.209 p.1337

Accidental hypothermia = involuntary drop in core body temperature below 35°C (95°F), associated with high morbidity and mortality.

Therapeutic hypothermia = also called targeted temperature management — performed deliberately after cardiac arrest, traumatic brain injury, etc.

Epidemiology

  • Hypothermia occurs in both cold and warm climates; cases reported even in tropical settings.
  • US estimate: 5 cases per 100,000 inhabitants in nontropical climates (per CDC/Tintinalli).
  • Mortality is highest in elderly, alcoholics, trauma victims, and those with severe comorbidities.

Primary vs Secondary Hypothermia

  • Primary: healthy individuals exposed to cold environment (e.g., outdoor workers, hikers, drowning victims).
  • Secondary: due to underlying disease, drug, or trauma — see Table 209-1 below.
📚 Table 209-1 — Causes of Secondary Hypothermia (Tintinalli p.1337)
Inline MCQ 1. A 65-year-old alcoholic male is found unresponsive on a sidewalk on a 12°C night. Rectal temperature 31°C. Which classification of hypothermia is this most consistent with?
A. Primary, mild (HT I)
B. Secondary, moderate (HT II)
C. Therapeutic hypothermia
D. Primary, severe (HT III)
Answer: B. Core temperature 28–32°C is moderate (HT II). Alcohol intoxication causes vasodilation and impaired thermoregulation, making this secondary hypothermia. Confused/impaired consciousness fits HT II. Reference: Tintinalli Table 209-1, 209-2, p.1337–1338.

2. Pathophysiology

Tintinalli p.1337–1338

Heat Loss Mechanisms

  • Conduction — direct contact (immersion in cold water, lying on cold ground): ~25× heat loss vs. air.
  • Convection — moving air/water carries heat away (wind chill); ↑↑ with wind & wet clothing.
  • Evaporation — sweat & insensible loss; significant in dry, windy conditions.
  • Radiation — infrared heat loss to cooler surroundings; significant if uncovered head/skin.

Heat Conservation & Production

  • Behavioral: putting on warm clothing, seeking shelter.
  • Peripheral vasoconstriction — limits convective and conductive heat loss.
  • Increased metabolic rate — sympathetic-driven thermogenesis.
  • Shivering — voluntary muscle contraction; increases metabolism by up to 5× resting rate. Lost when core temp drops below ~30–32°C.

Cold Physiology Effects

SystemEffects
CNSConfusion, ataxia, slurred speech (32–35°C); stupor, areflexia (28–32°C); coma, fixed pupils (<28°C).
CardiacBradycardia, ↑ QT, ↑ PR, ↑ QRS, Osborn (J) wave (Fig 209-1); atrial fibrillation common at 32°C; VF risk <28°C.
RespiratoryInitial tachypnea → progressive bradypnea; ↓ CO₂ production.
RenalCold-induced diuresis from peripheral vasoconstriction → relative hypovolemia.
CoagulationCoagulopathy from platelet dysfunction & sequestration; DIC risk.
Acid-baseVariable; lactic acidosis from poor perfusion ± respiratory acidosis.
📚 Fig 209-1 — ECG: bradycardia + slow ventricular response + Osborn (J) wave at 25°C (Tintinalli p.1339)
📌 Pearl — Osborn (J) wave: A characteristic positive deflection at the J point (after QRS, before ST). Most prominent in left precordial leads. Amplitude correlates with severity but not pathognomonic for hypothermia.
Inline MCQ 2. Which ECG finding is most characteristic of moderate-to-severe hypothermia?
A. Peaked T waves
B. ST elevation in V1–V3
C. U wave inversion
D. Osborn (J) wave
Answer: D. Osborn (J) wave is the classic finding. Peaked T = hyperkalemia; ST elevation can occur but isn't specific to hypothermia. Reference: Tintinalli Fig 209-1, p.1339.

3. Classification & Staging

Tintinalli Table 209-2 p.1338

The Swiss/Mountain Medicine classification (HT I–IV) is most clinically useful as it maps directly to treatment.

📚 Table 209-2 — Staging and Treatment of Accidental Hypothermia (Tintinalli p.1338)
StageCore TempHallmark
HT I — Mild32–35°CConscious, shivering
HT II — Moderate28–32°CImpaired consciousness; shivering may stop
HT III — Severe<28°CUnconscious, vital signs present
HT IV — Hypothermic cardiac arrestVariableNo vital signs; arrest below 32°C, ↑ risk <28°C
Clinical caveat: Consciousness can be impaired by comorbid illness (trauma, CNS pathology, toxic ingestion) independent of core temp. Don't rely on mental status alone.
Inline MCQ 3. A skier rescued from an avalanche has core temp 26°C, GCS 6, but a palpable femoral pulse at 30 bpm. Which Swiss stage?
A. HT I
B. HT II
C. HT III
D. HT IV
Answer: C. Core temp <28°C with vital signs present = HT III (severe). HT IV requires absent vital signs. Reference: Tintinalli Table 209-2.

4. Clinical Features

Tintinalli p.1339
  • Skin: cold to touch; cyanosis; "shovel sign" of frostbite if exposed.
  • Mental status: ranges from confusion → ataxic gait → stupor → coma. "Paradoxical undressing" may occur in severe hypothermia.
  • Cardiovascular: bradycardia disproportionate to BP; hypotension; J wave; arrhythmias (most commonly AF).
  • Respiratory: initial hyperventilation transitioning to slow shallow breathing.
  • Pupils: may be fixed and dilated below ~28°C — does NOT indicate brain death in hypothermia.
⚠️ Critical pitfall: "No one is dead until warm and dead." Resuscitation should not be terminated based on absent vital signs alone in hypothermic patients — many have been successfully resuscitated from core temperatures <15°C. Exceptions: obvious lethal injury, frozen body (chest noncompressible), valid DNR, prolonged avalanche burial >35 min with airway packed with snow, or potassium >12 mmol/L.

5. Diagnosis & Core Temperature Measurement

Tintinalli p.1339

Preferred temperature sites

  1. Esophageal probe (24 cm below larynx in intubated adult) — best for monitoring during rewarming and most accurately reflects cardiac temperature.
  2. Bladder (Foley with thermistor) — alternative if esophageal not feasible.
  3. Rectal — common but lags behind core during rewarming; insert ≥15 cm.
  4. Tympanic infrared — may be inaccurate in profound hypothermia.
Avoid: oral temps (unreliable), axillary (poor in low perfusion), and skin/forehead probes.

Lab Workup

  • CBC, full chemistry, magnesium, phosphate, glucose
  • Coagulation panel (PT/aPTT/INR; consider TEG if available) — coagulopathy is common
  • ABG (uncorrected for temp; alpha-stat strategy)
  • Lactate, troponin
  • Toxicology, ethanol
  • ECG (Osborn waves, AF, dysrhythmias)
  • Imaging as guided by mechanism (e.g., CT brain if trauma/altered mentation)
Inline MCQ 4. Which core temperature measurement is preferred for monitoring intubated patients during active rewarming?
A. Tympanic infrared
B. Esophageal probe at 24 cm
C. Rectal at 5 cm
D. Oral
Answer: B. Esophageal probe in lower 1/3 best reflects cardiac/core temp; reliable during active rewarming. Rectal lags. Tympanic and oral are unreliable in low perfusion. Reference: Tintinalli p.1339.

6. Treatment

Tintinalli p.1340–1342

General principles (all stages)

  1. Stop further heat loss — remove wet clothing, insulate, dry, shield from wind.
  2. Gentle handling — myocardium is irritable; rough movement can precipitate VF below 28°C.
  3. Horizontal position with airway management as needed.
  4. IV access — warm crystalloid (38–42°C); avoid LR (impaired hepatic metabolism of lactate).
  5. Treat underlying cause — toxin, trauma, sepsis, hypoglycemia.
  6. Continuous monitoring — ECG, core temp, end-tidal CO₂.

Stage-specific treatment

StageApproach
HT I (Mild)Passive external rewarming — warm environment, blankets, sweet drinks if alert; encourage active movement.
HT II (Moderate)Active external + minimally invasive rewarming (forced air, heating pads, warm IVF); cardiac monitoring.
HT III (Severe)HT II measures + airway management; preferentially treat at ECLS center due to high VF risk; consider ECLS for refractory hemodynamic instability.
HT IV (Cardiac arrest)CPR + defibrillation (up to 3 doses initially); transport to ECLS center; ECMO/CPB is definitive rewarming.
⚠️ Drug pharmacology in hypothermia:
• Most drugs have ↓ metabolism and may sequester in cold tissue.
• Below 30°C — typically withhold cardiac drugs (epinephrine, amiodarone) — they accumulate without effect, then become toxic on rewarming.
• 30–35°C — give drugs at extended intervals (every 6–10 min instead of 3–5).
• Defibrillation: up to 3 attempts; if unsuccessful, defer further shocks until core temp >30°C.
Inline MCQ 5. A patient in cardiac arrest with core temperature 26°C remains in VF after 3 defibrillation attempts. What is the most appropriate next step?
A. Continue standard ACLS shock-drug-shock-drug cycles
B. Give 3 doses of epinephrine 1 mg every 3–5 min
C. Defer further defibrillation, continue CPR, transport to ECLS center
D. Terminate resuscitation efforts
Answer: C. Below 30°C the heart is refractory to defibrillation and drugs accumulate. After 3 unsuccessful shocks, continue high-quality CPR and rewarm via ECMO/CPB at an ECLS-capable center. Reference: Tintinalli p.1342, ERC 2021 hypothermia guidelines.

7. Rewarming Strategies

Tintinalli p.1342–1343

Passive external rewarming

  • Warm dry environment (≥21°C), blankets, insulation.
  • Adequate for HT I if patient is shivering and otherwise stable.

Active external rewarming

  • Forced-air warming blankets (Bair Hugger), heating pads, warm-water immersion.
  • Apply to trunk only — limb rewarming first can cause "afterdrop" (cool peripheral blood returns to core).

Minimally invasive (active core) rewarming

  • Warm IV crystalloid (38–42°C, NOT LR).
  • Warm humidified O₂.
  • Bladder lavage (warm saline 38–42°C, 3-way Foley); peritoneal lavage; thoracic lavage.

Invasive / extracorporeal rewarming (ECLS)

  • VA ECMO or cardiopulmonary bypass — gold standard for HT III with hemodynamic instability and HT IV (arrest).
  • Rewarm 6–10°C/hour; monitor for "rewarming shock" (vasodilation + relative hypovolemia).
  • Hemodialysis — alternative if ECMO unavailable; less efficient.
📚 Fig 209-4 — Practical rewarming setup ("hypothermia burrito") (Tintinalli p.1343)
Afterdrop phenomenon: Continued core cooling after rescue, due to (1) peripheral vasodilation when warming the extremities flushes cold blood to the core, and (2) the physical lag of heat conduction. Mitigate by core-first rewarming and limited limb manipulation.
Inline MCQ 6. Which IV fluid should be avoided in hypothermic patients?
A. Normal saline (warmed)
B. Lactated Ringer's
C. D5W
D. Plasmalyte
Answer: B. Hepatic metabolism of lactate is impaired in hypothermia, leading to lactate accumulation. Use warmed NS or D5NS instead. Reference: Tintinalli p.1340.

8. Hypothermic Cardiac Arrest (HT IV)

Tintinalli Fig 209-2, 209-3
📚 Fig 209-2 — Transport and management algorithm for accidental hypothermia (Tintinalli p.1340)

Decision rules for ECLS transport vs termination of resuscitation (TOR)

  • Withhold/terminate CPR if any: decapitation, decomposition, truncal transection, body frozen solid (chest noncompressible), valid DNR.
  • If avalanche burial ≤35 min, or unwitnessed arrest with hypothermia plausible — continue CPR.
  • If avalanche burial >35 min with airway packed with snow → consider TOR (likely asphyxial cardiac arrest pre-hypothermia).
  • Serum K⁺ >12 mmol/L → death prior to cooling; TOR is appropriate.
  • Serum K⁺ <12 mmol/L → potentially salvageable; transport to ECLS.
📚 Fig 209-3 — Triage algorithm: HT patients with absent vital signs (Tintinalli p.1342)

ECLS rewarming criteria (per ICAR-MEDCOM)

📚 Table 209-3 — ECLS criteria for severe hypothermia (Tintinalli p.1344)
Inline MCQ 7. An avalanche victim is found in cardiac arrest after 50 min of burial. Airway is patent, K⁺ = 7 mmol/L. Best management?
A. Terminate resuscitation — burial >35 min
B. Ground transport to nearest ED
C. CPR + transport to ECMO/CPB-capable center
D. Rewarm to 32°C in field then assess
Answer: C. With patent airway and K⁺ <12, hypothermic cardiac arrest is potentially salvageable. Continue CPR and transport to an ECLS center. Reference: Tintinalli Fig 209-3, p.1342.
Inline MCQ 8. Which serum potassium level represents the threshold above which prognosis after hypothermic arrest is considered nonsurvivable?
A. >5 mmol/L
B. >7 mmol/L
C. >10 mmol/L
D. >12 mmol/L
Answer: D. K⁺ >12 mmol/L is the threshold supporting termination of resuscitation. Reference: Tintinalli Table 209-3, ERC 2021 guidelines.

9. Special Populations & Pitfalls

Tintinalli p.1343–1344

Pediatric considerations

  • Higher surface-area-to-volume ratio → more rapid cooling.
  • Best reported pediatric survival from cardiac arrest at core temp 13.7°C (drowning, ECMO rewarming).

Elderly

  • Impaired thermoregulation, reduced subcutaneous fat, polypharmacy (β-blockers, sedatives).
  • "Urban" hypothermia from inadequate heating common; mortality higher than younger patients.

Trauma patients

  • "Lethal triad": hypothermia + acidosis + coagulopathy → high mortality.
  • Active rewarming during massive transfusion is critical; warm all fluids and products.

Drowning

  • If hypothermic arrest from cold-water drowning before hypoxic arrest, ECMO rewarming may yield neurologically intact survival.
  • If hypoxia preceded cooling, prognosis is poor.

⚕️ ATLS 11th Edition — Hypothermia in Trauma

ATLS Ch.10 Cold Injuries / Trauma in Cold Environments

ATLS classifies trauma-associated hypothermia separately because of its impact on the "lethal triad" (hypothermia + coagulopathy + acidosis):

SeverityCore tempATLS-specific implications
Mild36–34°CCoagulation already affected; warm all blood products and IVF.
Moderate34–32°CSignificant coagulopathy; consider damage-control surgery; ↑ blood transfusion need.
Severe<32°CProfound coagulopathy; DIC risk; may require ECMO if persistent acidosis & instability.

ATLS rewarming priorities in trauma

  1. Prevent further heat loss — remove wet clothing, dry, increase ambient room temperature to ≥28°C.
  2. Warm IV fluids and blood products to 39°C (use rapid blood-warming infusers).
  3. Active external rewarming — forced-air blankets, heating pads on torso.
  4. Damage control surgery if profound coagulopathy or core temp <32°C.
  5. ECMO/CPB for refractory cases per institutional capability.
ATLS pitfall: Even mild hypothermia (<36°C) doubles mortality in major trauma. Warm everything that touches the patient — IV fluids, blood products, ventilator gas, room.

📗 Rosen's Emergency Medicine 10th — Accidental Hypothermia

Rosen's Ch.131

Rosen's emphasis points

  • Definitions — Rosen's uses the same Swiss/Mountain Medicine HT I–IV staging adopted by Tintinalli.
  • Core temp measurement: esophageal preferred for active rewarming; rectal acceptable but lags.
  • Drug therapy: Rosen's specifically supports standard ACLS algorithms with epinephrine and defibrillation when core ≥30°C; below 30°C, drugs may be given but at extended intervals.
  • Hyperkalemia threshold for nonsurvivable arrest: Rosen's cites K⁺ >10–12 mmol/L (range, with 12 being the most accepted upper limit).
  • ECMO criteria: failure of standard rewarming, hemodynamic instability, refractory dysrhythmia, K⁺ <12, no signs of incompatibility with life.

Comparison: Tintinalli vs Rosen's

TopicTintinalli Ch.209Rosen's Ch.131
Drug thresholdWithhold below 30°CExtended intervals below 30°C; allowed
DefibrillationUp to 3 attempts initiallyUp to 3 below 30°C; resume above 30°C
K⁺ futility cutoff>12 mmol/L>10–12 mmol/L
Preferred core temp siteEsophagealEsophageal (lower 1/3)
ECMO indicationHT III refractory + HT IVHT III refractory + HT IV; +/- avalanche <35 min
Bottom line: Both textbooks agree on the core principles: gentle handling, prevent afterdrop, treat secondary causes, ECMO for refractory severe cases. Differences are mostly in drug-administration timing.

End MCQ 1. A 45-year-old hiker is brought to the ED with rectal temp 30°C. He is shivering, GCS 13, BP 110/70. Which Swiss stage?
A. HT I
B. HT II
C. HT III
D. HT IV
Answer: B. Core temp 28–32°C with impaired consciousness = HT II (moderate). Note shivering may be present or absent in HT II.
End MCQ 2. Which of the following is the most accurate statement about defibrillation in hypothermic cardiac arrest?
A. Defibrillate continuously every 2 min regardless of temp
B. Up to 3 shocks if VF; further attempts deferred until core ≥30°C
C. Avoid defibrillation entirely below 28°C
D. Defibrillation is contraindicated in hypothermia
Answer: B. Per ERC/AHA: up to 3 attempts initially; if unsuccessful below 30°C, defer further shocks and rewarm. Reference: Tintinalli p.1342.
End MCQ 3. Which fluid should be given to a hypothermic patient requiring resuscitation?
A. Lactated Ringer's at room temp
B. Lactated Ringer's warmed to 42°C
C. 0.9% NS warmed to 38–42°C
D. Half NS at room temp
Answer: C. Warm NS (38–42°C) is preferred. Avoid LR — impaired hepatic lactate metabolism in hypothermia.
End MCQ 4. Which population is at highest risk for 'urban hypothermia' even in temperate climates?
A. Young athletes
B. Elderly with inadequate heating
C. Children
D. Outdoor laborers
Answer: B. Elderly patients have impaired thermoregulation, reduced fat insulation, and may live in inadequately heated dwellings. Tintinalli Table 209-1.
End MCQ 5. A patient pulled from a frozen lake has core temp 22°C and asystole. Serum K⁺ = 9 mmol/L. What is the next best step?
A. Terminate resuscitation
B. Continue CPR and transport to ECLS center
C. Rewarm passively in the ED only
D. Open chest cardiac massage in the ED
Answer: B. K⁺ <12 with hypothermic arrest is salvageable; ECMO is gold-standard rewarming. Reference: Fig 209-3.
End MCQ 6. The Osborn (J) wave on ECG is best described as:
A. ST elevation in inferior leads
B. Positive deflection at the J point most prominent in left precordial leads
C. QRS widening with right bundle branch morphology
D. Inverted T waves in V1–V3
Answer: B. Osborn wave = positive J-point deflection, most prominent in V3–V6 in moderate-severe hypothermia.
End MCQ 7. Which intervention is contraindicated in HT III hypothermia patients?
A. Endotracheal intubation
B. Femoral central line
C. Aggressive limb manipulation
D. Warm IV fluids
Answer: C. Below 28°C the myocardium is irritable. Rough handling (chest compressions excepted) can precipitate VF. Avoid unnecessary movement of limbs early.
End MCQ 8. Which is the most reliable site for monitoring core temperature during active rewarming?
A. Tympanic membrane infrared
B. Esophageal probe at the lower 1/3
C. Forehead skin probe
D. Oral thermometer
Answer: B. Esophageal probe in the lower 1/3 best reflects cardiac/blood temp during rewarming.
End MCQ 9. Which clinical feature suggests 'paradoxical undressing'?
A. A hypothermic patient is found nude despite ambient cold
B. A patient has cold, mottled hands
C. Warm trunk with cold extremities
D. Cyanosis of the lips
Answer: A. Paradoxical undressing — patients with severe hypothermia may remove clothing due to a sensation of warmth from peripheral vasodilation in late cooling.
End MCQ 10. Which is the most appropriate monitoring for a patient with HT II being actively rewarmed?
A. Intermittent BP only
B. Continuous ECG, core temp, end-tidal CO₂
C. Pulse oximetry alone
D. Hourly oral temp
Answer: B. All HT II patients require continuous ECG (arrhythmia risk), accurate core temp, and end-tidal CO₂ monitoring.
End MCQ 11. Which statement about drug administration in hypothermic cardiac arrest at 27°C is correct?
A. Standard ACLS dosing every 3–5 min
B. Drugs may be withheld until core temp >30°C
C. Double standard doses
D. Subcutaneous administration preferred
Answer: B. Below 30°C drugs accumulate without effect and become toxic on rewarming. Many guidelines recommend withholding until ≥30°C.
End MCQ 12. Which condition is NOT considered an obvious sign of irreversible death in a hypothermic patient?
A. Decapitation
B. Truncal transection
C. Body frozen solid with noncompressible chest
D. Fixed and dilated pupils
Answer: D. Pupils may be fixed and dilated below 28°C without indicating brain death. Decapitation, transection, frozen body — all confirmed irreversible.
End MCQ 13. In severe hypothermic patients with cardiac instability, the gold-standard rewarming method is:
A. Warm bladder lavage
B. Forced-air blankets
C. Veno-arterial ECMO/CPB
D. Hot oral fluids
Answer: C. VA ECMO or CPB provide simultaneous circulatory support and rapid rewarming (6–10°C/h).
End MCQ 14. A trauma patient with core temp 33°C, INR 1.8, pH 7.21, and ongoing hemorrhage best fits which physiologic state?
A. Hypothermic shock only
B. The 'lethal triad' of hypothermia, coagulopathy, acidosis
C. Septic shock
D. Distributive shock
Answer: B. Hypothermia + coagulopathy + acidosis = lethal triad; mandates damage-control resuscitation and warming everything.
End MCQ 15. Which of the following best characterizes 'afterdrop' phenomenon?
A. Drop in BP after defibrillation
B. Continued decline in core temperature after rescue from cold environment
C. Drop in core temp after rapid extremity rewarming due to cold venous return
D. B and C are both correct
Answer: D. Both B (continued cooling after rescue) and C (cold venous return) describe afterdrop mechanisms.
End MCQ 16. Which ECG abnormality is LEAST likely in moderate hypothermia (28–32°C)?
A. Bradycardia disproportionate to BP
B. Atrial fibrillation
C. ST elevation V1–V3 (Brugada-like)
D. Acute right bundle branch block (new)
Answer: D. New RBBB is not a typical hypothermia finding. Bradycardia, AF, J-waves, ST changes are characteristic.
End MCQ 17. Which of the following is recommended for prevention of afterdrop?
A. Rapid limb-first rewarming with warm-water immersion
B. Core-first active rewarming with limb insulation
C. Cold-water immersion of trunk
D. Aggressive limb massage
Answer: B. Core-first warming reduces peripheral vasodilation that returns cold blood to the core.
End MCQ 18. Which is the most appropriate setting for HT IV (cardiac arrest) management?
A. Local community ED
B. Trauma center without ECMO
C. ECLS-capable center with ECMO/CPB
D. Closest urgent care
Answer: C. HT IV requires ECMO/CPB for definitive rewarming; transport to ECLS center is preferred per Fig 209-3.
End MCQ 19. Which is true about pediatric drowning + hypothermic cardiac arrest?
A. Always futile
B. Best prognosis if hypothermia preceded hypoxia
C. Best prognosis if hypoxia preceded hypothermia
D. ECMO is contraindicated
Answer: B. If cooling occurred before hypoxic injury, neurologic recovery is possible. Cases of full recovery from core temp 13.7°C are reported.
End MCQ 20. Which statement reflects the 2021 ERC hypothermia guidelines?
A. Terminate CPR after 30 min in all hypothermic arrests
B. K⁺ >12 mmol/L supports termination of resuscitation
C. ECMO is reserved only for in-hospital arrest
D. Standard ACLS without modification
Answer: B. K⁺ >12 indicates death prior to cooling; supports TOR. Otherwise rewarm to ≥32°C before terminating.

🔑 Key Points (High-Yield)

  1. Definition: Accidental hypothermia = involuntary core temp <35°C. Primary (exposure) vs Secondary (disease/drugs).
  2. Swiss staging drives therapy: HT I (35–32°C), HT II (32–28°C), HT III (<28°C), HT IV (cardiac arrest).
  3. Osborn (J) wave on ECG = positive deflection at J point — characteristic of moderate-severe hypothermia.
  4. Core temp: esophageal > bladder > rectal. Avoid oral/tympanic/skin probes.
  5. "No one is dead until warm and dead" — except: obvious lethal injury, body frozen solid (chest noncompressible), valid DNR, K⁺ >12, avalanche >35 min with airway packed with snow.
  6. Drug pharmacology: Below 30°C — withhold cardiac drugs; defibrillation up to 3× then defer until ≥30°C.
  7. IVF: Warm 0.9% NS at 38–42°C. Avoid LR (impaired lactate metabolism).
  8. Afterdrop mitigated by core-first active rewarming.
  9. VA ECMO/CPB = gold standard for HT III refractory + HT IV.
  10. K⁺ >12 mmol/L = death prior to cooling; TOR appropriate.
  11. Lethal triad in trauma: hypothermia + coagulopathy + acidosis. Warm everything (room ≥28°C, IVF, blood, ventilator gas).
  12. Pediatric prognosis in cold-water drowning can be excellent if cooling preceded hypoxia.
